title: GitHub and Remote Repositories
summary: Shows how to publish a local Git repository to GitHub: create an empty repository in the browser, link it with git remote add origin, upload the history with git push -u origin main, and view commits on GitHub. Recaps the local pipeline (working directory, staging, local repo) and where the remote fits.

concepts.heading: Remote repositories and GitHub
points: A remote repository is a copy of the project hosted on another machine; GitHub is the hosting service used in the course. It is free; create an account at github.com and confirm the email address.
Create a repo in the browser: use the + menu at the top right, choose New repository, give it a name (the demo reuses the local folder name, Story) and an optional description.
Visibility: Public means anyone can see every committed file; Private restricts access. Public repos are useful for learning from others' code and for contributing to open-source projects.
Leave 'initialize with a README' unticked when pushing an existing local repo, so the remote starts empty and there are no conflicting commits.

After creation, GitHub shows setup instructions. The command-line route (push an existing repository) is the one used in the lesson; the GitHub Desktop client is an alternative the instructor does not use.

concepts.heading: Connecting local to remote
points: Run commands from inside the local project folder (the working directory). git log first confirms which commits exist, two in the demo.

git remote add origin <URL>: registers a remote called origin pointing at the GitHub repository URL copied from the page. The name is arbitrary, but origin is the standard convention and recommended so others recognise it.

git push -u origin main: uploads the commits of the local main branch to the remote named origin. The -u flag (upstream) links the local branch to the remote one so later you can simply run git push or git pull.
main is the default branch: the linear chain of save points. Branches are covered in a later lesson.
Success is signalled by the prompt returning and a message that the local main now tracks the remote main from origin. Upload time depends on repository size.
(Extra) Older Git setups may create the first branch as master; git branch -M main renames the current branch so it matches GitHub's default. GitHub's setup page lists this command too.

concepts.heading: Viewing the result on GitHub
points: Refreshing the repo page shows all the files with their latest commit messages.
The Commits list shows each save point and its time; opening one shows exactly which lines changed in that commit.
Insights then Network (the graph view) draws the main branch with one node per commit; hovering shows each message.
Hosting history on GitHub also helps for non-code projects, such as writing, since any earlier version can be seen or restored.

concepts.heading: Mental model
points: Local flow: working directory, git add into the staging area, git commit into the local repository, building a main branch timeline.
Remote: a parallel repository on GitHub. Local and remote can differ; git push sends local commits to the remote, which is what syncs them.
In the demo the local repo is the .git folder in Story and the remote is the GitHub project that stores all the commits.

code_examples.caption: Push an existing local repo to a new empty GitHub repo
code_examples.code:
cd ~/Desktop/Story
git log                                            # confirm the local commits
git remote add origin https://github.com/<user>/Story.git
git branch -M main                                 # only if your branch is not already called main
git push -u origin main                            # upload commits and link the branches

code_examples.caption: (Extra) Useful follow-up commands
code_examples.code:
git remote -v      # list configured remotes and their URLs
git push           # later pushes need no arguments after -u
git pull           # fetch and merge new commits from origin

pitfalls: Ticking 'add a README' on GitHub before pushing an existing project, which leads to a rejected push because the histories differ.
Pasting the wrong URL or running the commands outside the project folder.
Anything committed to a public repository is public, including secrets; the next lesson (.gitignore) addresses this.
(Extra) Authentication: pushing over HTTPS requires a personal access token or a credential helper rather than the account password.

gaps_and_ideas: Extend the proposed Git playground lesson with a 'remote' step: a visual of two repositories (local and GitHub) where git remote add and git push -u animate commits moving across.
Task idea: given a list of commands in the wrong order, put the push-existing-repo sequence in the correct order.
